extractor_prompt.instructions:
Extract every claim the response below makes, as triplets: (subject | predicate | object).

Basic rules:
- A claim is one triplet. Extract every claim the response makes, right or wrong; never correct, repair or complete it.
- Use the response's own words. Add nothing it does not contain: no new holder, hedge, quantity, modal or verb. A word may change its form (tense, number, part of speech), not its meaning; joining words (is, are, has, of, for, in, on, at, that, articles) are allowed.
- Every triplet must read alone, without the response: resolve references from the response itself.

The situations below decide everything else. Each line is one rule.

Assertion, presupposition and speech act
- Talk about the text or the answer itself: A sentence about the response itself, not about the topic, gives no claim: words that organise the text (“here is the answer”, “in summary”, “key points”), a frame that names the response's source (“based on the information provided”), what the response, its sources or its author is or is not (“I am an AI assistant”, “this may not be accurate”, “this is not medical advice”, “the passages focus mainly on …”), and a sign-off (“I hope this helps”). Remarks to or about the user or the conversation (“you may be thinking of …”, “I apologize for my mistake”) give no claim either. A stance of the sources against content (“other passages express skepticism about X”) is not such talk: it gives (X | is | doubted). The content such a frame introduces is extracted as usual. A source frame drops only when the content after it is about the world; when it is about evidence or knowledge (“based on the passages, there is no clear evidence that …”, “… it is unclear whether …”), the sentence says what the passages lack and gives no claim. Advice to the reader stays advice even when it is about the answer (“do not rely on this alone”). A disclaimer about the whole answer does not weaken the claims around it. Pure emphasis (“of course”, “obviously”, “naturally”, “indeed”) is dropped; a word that says how the speaker knows (“evidently”, “apparently”) or how sure they are (“definitely”, “probably”) stays in the claim.
- A question in the response: A question gives no claim, whatever it is for, including an offer to the reader (“Would you like more details?”) and a rhetorical question. The response's answer to its own question is extracted as stated, read with that question: “Do cats purr only when happy? No: …” gives (cats | do not purr only when | they are happy).
- Assumed background: What a sentence only takes for granted is not a claim of its own, unless the response adds new information there (a date, a name, a number): “the ban they imposed in 2019” gives (the commissioners | imposed the burn ban in | 2019). A factive verb (“know that”, “discovered that”, “realised that”) takes its complement as true: the complement is a claim of its own, next to the claim about the holder: “Residents know that the vote is on Monday” gives (residents | know that | the vote is on Monday) and (the vote | is on | Monday). A non-factive verb (“believe that”, “claim that”) does not. A source with a reporting verb that passes its content on as fact (“tests show that”) stays one claim.
- What the wording suggests: Extract what the response says, not what its wording suggests. A limit it states outright (“only some”, “not all”, “no other”) is part of the claim. One named exception: a threshold or condition stated as a rule is the rule.
- Vague statements about the world: A statement about the world is a claim even when it is vague, and even when it is about what is known (“more research is needed”, “experts disagree”). A sentence that announces a list but says something about the topic (“there are several factors to consider:”) is a claim; one that only points at the text (“here are the factors:”) is not. Content passed on from the sources is the response’s own claim: “the sources describe several uses of borax” gives (borax | has | several uses).
- An abstention: A sentence that says the response or its passages leave something open gives no claim, whether it covers part of the question or all of it: what the passages or the information given lack (“the passages do not say whether …”, “there is no information on …”, “the passages conflict”, “the evidence does not clearly indicate whether …” when the evidence is the material the response was given), what the response cannot settle itself (“I do not know whether …”, “the evidence in the passages is mixed, so it is hard to say”), or what would settle it (“more information would help draw a firmer conclusion”, “more data would be needed to be sure”). Everything else in the response is extracted. Doubt about the world with nothing that points at the response is a claim: (whether hedgehogs eat snails | is | unclear); “more research is needed”; “experts disagree”.
- A judgement: A judgement is a claim, in the response's own strength. A judgement inside a noun phrase (“the vital canal”) is split off as its own claim, and the host claim is stated without it. An exclamation is classified by what it says, not by its punctuation: a judgement about the topic is a claim, while praise of the response itself follows filler. A sentence adverb that judges its whole event (“unfortunately”, “surprisingly”) becomes a judgement of that event, using the adverb’s adjective form and the event’s own words; the event is extracted without it. Do not invent “I think” or a new holder. The judgement is not supported merely because the event is.
- Advice and instructions: An imperative is the one sentence with no claim form of its own, so it takes one fixed form: its understood subject “you” and “should”, every other word as written: (you | should seal | your grout once a year), (you | should never use | bleach on coloured grout). A sentence with its own subject keeps it as written, with its own strength word: (grout | can be sealed | once a year), (you | can reduce your heating bill by | insulating the loft). A caveat or disclaimer is advice too and takes the same form: “As always, consult your doctor or pharmacist” gives (you | should consult | your doctor or pharmacist). A sentence about the answer itself (“this is not medical advice”) gives no claim; advice about what to do with the answer (“do not rely on this alone”) is advice like any other. A first-person recommendation (“I recommend that you …”, “I suggest …”, “I advise …”) keeps its own words and counts as advice at “should” strength: (I | recommend that you seal | your grout once a year). Generic “one” in reader advice keeps that subject and its written strength; “one should” is advice to the reader, and “you must” is an obligation. In an answer about what to do, “can” is advice at its weakest strength (“grout can be sealed once a year”); a “can” that states what something is able to do is “Ability, permission and obligation”, and “may” as possibility is hedge.
- An imagined case or worked example: An imagined case is one conditional claim, its assumption inside: (a car bought for $30,000 | would be worth after a year | about $25,000). Its invented premise is never a claim of its own. A counterfactual (“had …, would have …”) is also one conditional claim: keep its condition and consequence together. Do not add the condition’s negation as an actual event merely because the wording suggests it; an actual event stated separately is extracted separately.
- A response that contradicts itself: Extract every assertion as stated, right or wrong, never repaired. A statement the response itself takes back is not asserted.
- Code, formulas and commands: Keep each written formula as one complete relation and each code listing as one text value under its supplied heading or surrounding prose. A recommended command uses the advice form, (you | should … | …), and retains flags and arguments. A block without a heading is still extracted; do not turn a listing into invented claims about execution or results.
- An ironic statement: When the response’s own words make irony unmistakable, the literal ironic judgement gives no claim; keep every separately asserted fact or judgement in its own words. Do not invent the opposite as a claim. Without an unmistakable cue, take praise at its word, even if it seems unlikely.
- A figure of speech: Keep a metaphor, idiom or clear hyperbole in the response’s own words as one assertion, including the words that identify its subject and scope. Do not replace the expression with an extractor-invented paraphrase, or discard it as non-factual. Actual measurements stay literal; where wording leaves the meaning unclear, do not invent a precise interpretation.
- Output not composed as an answer: Text that is not composed as an answer gives no claim: an echo of the question, a page label, site name or headline, a song line or other quoted line that says nothing about the world, and stray tokens. A declarative sentence about the world is a claim wherever it stands, however broken the text around it; a statement repeated in a loop is one claim, and an unfinished one gives nothing beyond its complete part. A response is never dropped whole for being degenerate.
- Content composed on request: A poem, story, rewritten lyrics or sample dialogue the response composes, on request or labelled as its own (“here is my version”), is not put forward as information and gives no claim. Lines the response presents as an existing work’s text are a quotation claim about that work: (Harbour Lights | opens with the lines | “…”). A statement about the work outside the composition (its author, its year) is a claim as usual.
- “Managed to” and “failed to”: Keep an implicative verb as written: (the Kestrel expedition | managed to reach | the summit of Mount Arden). It states its result: “managed to X” and “succeeded in X-ing” state X, “failed to X” states that X did not happen. The effort or attempt the verb takes for granted is not a claim of its own: it stays inside the verb, which the claim keeps, and is not checked. A verb that only reports an attempt or a wish (“tried to”, “hoped to”, “planned to”) states nothing about the result.

Evidentiality and attribution
- Someone else's view: Someone else's view keeps its holder: (holder | says / argues / believes | the whole view). A fact said in passing is the response's own plain claim. A second holder around the first frames the whole: (the local paper | reports that | critics expect …). A vague or collective holder (“experts”, “it is widely believed”) stays exactly as written, with any agreement or frequency word inside the reported claim. “Experts agree that X” is one attributed claim, not an extra claim that a consensus exists. An explicit agreement is stronger than merely reporting that some people hold the view; do not erase that distinction. “Studies show” follows “How strongly a reporting verb puts its content” rather than being flattened into a belief. A named holder (a named person, organisation, publication or dated study) stays as written like any other holder.
- References to the passages: Nothing that points to the material the response was given is part of a claim: no passage number, citation marker, count of passages (“most passages”) or noun for that material (“the passages”, “the evidence”, “the information” when it means the material). By default the response passes the content on as its own: “Passage 4 notes that X”, “the information lists X” and “X (Passage 2)” all give the plain claim X. Where the response keeps its distance, the content takes a fixed form without the source: content put as only suggested (“Passage 4 suggests X”, and “the evidence indicates X” or “the information indicates X” summing up the material, the response’s own inference; one passage that “indicates X” passes X on) gives (that X | is | suggested); content the response marks as not adopted (it sets it against contrary content, or calls it doubtful or someone’s claim) gives (that X | is | stated); a stance of the material against content (“other passages express skepticism about X”) gives (X | is | doubted), without “that” before a noun phrase. When the response reports passages that disagree, each side is its own claim in these forms. A judgement about a source gives a claim only if it states or hedges a statement about the world: “the figure of 27 appears outdated” gives (the Air Force enlistment age figure of 27 | appears | outdated), with “the figure” resolved from the response, while “Passage 3 is unclear” gives none; a report that the matter is open (“the passages conflict on X”) gives no claim. “Suggests” meaning “recommends” takes the advice form. A URL used only as a citation marker drops with that marker. A statement locating information at a named resource (“fees are listed at …”) is an ordinary claim and keeps the address as written; an instruction to visit it follows instruction. A bare link takes a supplied label, never an invented description of what the page contains.
- How strongly a reporting verb puts its content: Keep a reporting verb as written, with its source: (research | suggests that | houseplants take some pollutants out of indoor air). The verb sets the strength: “show”, “find”, “confirm” pass the content on as fact; “suggest”, “imply”, “point to” make it only possible; “indicate” passes the content on when its subject is a text (a report, an article, a passage) and makes it only possible when its subject is evidence or data; “say”, “argue”, “claim” report a view (attribution). Never rewrite the verb into a hedge, never drop it. When the source is the material the response was given, nothing that points to it stays: “Passage 2 states X” and “Passage 2 indicates X” give the plain claim X; “Passage 1 suggests X”, and “the evidence indicates X” or “the information indicates X” summing up the material, give (that X | is | suggested).
- “Allegedly”, “reportedly”, “apparently”: Keep the evidential adverb as written, in the predicate: (the mayor | allegedly accepted | gifts from a developer). “Allegedly” and “reportedly” mark someone else's statement; “apparently” and “evidently” say what the evidence shows.
- Quotations: Keep quotation marks where the response puts them. A person's words are their statement, (person | says / calls / describes … as | “content”), judged as their view. A quoted passage given as evidence is the response's own plain claim (the passage goes). Words in scare quotes stay inside the claim they stand in, as someone else's term: (the “miracle cure” diet | helped participants … lose | …).

Modality, quantity and precision
- Uncertainty: Keep the hedge at its strength, in the predicate, and copy it into every item it governs. Never add one and never drop one. A first-person “I think”, “I believe” or “I suspect” is a hedge on its clause: keep it as written, with the author as subject, (I | think that | X), read as the author’s own X at about the strength of “probably”; in front of a list it governs every item. “I know X” is a plain assertion.
- An approximate number: Keep the approximation word with its number. “About X” covers X plus or minus the larger of 10% and half the step of X's last non-zero digit; an exact number covers what rounds to it. Keep an explicit margin with its central value and unit; an unqualified “X ± d” gives those written bounds, not the default “about” tolerance. Keep a named confidence interval and its confidence level inside the statistical estimate. A confidence interval is not a spread of individual observations or a guarantee that the true value lies inside; a bare point estimate does not establish a reported confidence interval.
- A range: A range is one claim, as written. A plain range says the value lies somewhere in it; “ranges from”, “varies from”, “as little as” also claim that the ends occur.
- A bound: Keep the bound word with the number, as written. “Over” and “more than” exclude the number; “at least” and “or older” include it.
- How many, how often: Keep the quantifier or frequency word at its strength, in the subject or the predicate. Never add one and never drop one. Keep generic “people” and “one” as written too: an explicit “often” or “always” remains part of that claim, not a universal subject or advice. In a statement about service availability, retain that scope rather than turning it into a claim about how frequently each person acts. A vague numeral is a quantifier too, read by its usual span: a couple 2, a few 3 to 5, several 3 to 7, dozens 24 or more; it is never normalised to a number.
- A bare plural: Keep a bare plural bare and read it as a generic about the kind: it allows exceptions. It is found in “most”, “usually”, “typically”, “generally”; not in “some”, “many” or “a few”. One named exception: a generic about a danger (carries a disease, bites, stings, is poisonous) says only that members can have it, and is found in “some” or “a few”.
- A degree word: Keep the degree word where it modifies. Never add one and never drop one.
- A statistical value: Keep the response’s name for the statistic with its value, outcome, population and any stated comparison. Do not turn a summary into an individual value, equate risk with odds, or invent an absolute rate. A relative-risk statement remains a claim without a numerical baseline or named comparison group; keep its stated scope and never fill the omission.
- Ability, permission and obligation: Keep the response's modal and its meaning: capacity (“can lift”), permission (“are permitted to”) and an obligation on someone other than the reader (“applicants must be residents”) stay distinct from each other and are never turned into an asserted occurrence. A possibility (“may”, “might”, “could” meaning possibly) is a hedge, with its own scale (Uncertainty). Reader advice (“you should”, “you must register”) is advice (Advice and instructions).

Negation, polarity and exclusion
- A negation: Keep the negation as written, where the response puts it, with its scope words: “will not directly kill”, “kills none of them directly”, “nobody under 18 may apply”. Never move it, never reword it. Carry it into every item it covers: under “not”, “A or B” gives one negative claim per item. Keep “not uncommon”, “not impossible” and “not without” intact; do not strengthen them into an unqualified positive. Keep negation and its quantifier in their written order: “not every” is not “none”. If “all … not” remains ambiguous, preserve the full wording rather than choosing a reading. A “not X but Y” correction states the negative and the positive as separate claims, with their shared subject and verb restored from the sentence; an explicit retraction follows “A response that contradicts itself”.
- An exception: Keep the exception inside the one claim. Never split the rule from its exception: the rule alone overgeneralises.
- “Only”: Keep “only”, “just”, “solely” where they stand, inside the claim. Never add one and never drop one. A cleft (“It is electric trains that …”) keeps its focus as written; its “no one else” is an implicature, not part of the claim, unless “only” is said.
- “Need not”, “must not”, “may not”: Keep the response's own modal and negation words in their order (“need not”, “must not”, “may not”, “cannot”); do not reword them to settle their meaning.

Coordination and plurality
- List of items: One claim per item. Keep the items together when they only work together (a mix, a pair, “both”), and when they name the members of a definite plural (“the X are A and B”, a bare list answering “which X …”): that claim says these are all, so one wrong or missing member sinks it.
- Items that only hold together: Do not split items that only hold together: a shared value, a sum, a blend, a comparison or relation between the items, a pair (“both”). Test: read each part alone; split only if it says what the response says, with nothing lost and nothing that held only for the items together.
- Alternatives (A or B): Keep “A or B” whole, except under an operator that makes it apply to each item: a negation (not, never, no, without), the condition of an “if”, or a permission (can, may: “you may bring a laptop or a tablet” allows each). There, one claim per item, each with the operator. First ask whether the “or” gives a second name (alias) or one definition.
- A class with examples: One claim per example, the class inside: (the stall | sells | dried fruits such as figs). No membership claims, unless membership is what the sentence says (“examples of aggravated DUI include repeat offences”). “Some examples include” is not a hedge.
- Paired lists: Pair the items in order, one claim per pair. Never the cross product of the two lists.
- An open list (“etc.”): “Etc.”, “and more”, “among others” are not items: split the list, one claim per named item. A list made complete (“the only things”, “just these three”) is one claim with its “only”.

Modification and subordination
- A detail that adds a fact: A detail that adds a fact (an apposition, a non-restrictive relative clause, a parenthesis, a title before a name) is a claim of its own, the thing named in full; the host claim is stated without it. Test: without it, the claim is about the same thing and still true.
- A detail that says which thing is meant: Keep a restriction inside the one claim: (trains with diesel engines | are banned from | the tunnel). Test: without it, would the claim be about other things or say more? A detail that only adds a fact about things already identified is split off. A modifier that could belong to either of two nouns (“trains carrying lorries with diesel engines”) stays inside the complete phrase as written; it is resolved only when the response’s own wording fixes it, never from outside knowledge. An adjective that says the thing is not, or is no longer, what the noun names (“former”, “fake”, “toy”, “imitation”) is not a restriction: it names something else, so former diesel trains are not a narrower group of diesel trains. Keep it as written, inside the claim.
- A condition: Keep the condition inside the one claim (if, when, once, unless, depending on, a deadline with “by”). Never the bare statement plus a separate condition claim. “Even if” is no condition: “q even if p” asserts q in every case, p included, so the clause stays inside the one claim, (q | even if | p), and p itself is not a claim.
- What an action is for: Split a purpose off as its own claim, in the response's own words, every reference resolved: “it works best that way” gives (the fertilizer | works best | spread when the weather is dry). The advice is stated without it, in the advice form, (you | should … | …). Drop test: without the purpose, is the advice still true as meant? If not, the purpose is a condition of the advice and stays inside: (you | should return | unopened bags within 30 days to get a refund). Under a negation or prohibition the purpose stays inside too.
- Cause and effect: Attach each effect to the cause the response names; never a chain the response does not state, never reversed. A chain the response states gives one claim per stated link. Events joined by a bare “so” or “therefore” are each a claim, but the link between them states no cause. A reason that is a fact of its own is its own claim. Weaker causal words (“linked to”, “may contribute to”) stay as written.
- “Although”, “but”: One claim per clause; the contrast word (although, but, while, however) gives no claim.
- By what means, in what manner: Keep the means, instrument or manner inside the claim it modifies, in the response's own words. A sentence with its own subject keeps it, a generic “you” included: (you | can reduce your heating bill by | insulating the loft). Only an imperative, which has no subject, takes the advice form, (you | should … | …).

Reference, deixis and context dependence
- A word that points to something: Resolve every reference from the response itself; add nothing from the world. Name a sense, with the response's own head noun, only where the response gives the word two senses. A reference the response never resolves stays as written.
- A frame: place, day, heading: Copy a place, date, product or heading set once into every claim it governs, in the fixed form a label with its value takes: (the forecast for Ashby on Saturday | is | dry and sunny). The frame is part of the claim; it is never a claim of its own. A stated relation between events (“after the merger”, “before the opening”) is a time frame kept inside the event it locates. A separately asserted event is extracted separately, but the time phrase alone is not split into an extra occurrence claim or a causal link. Ordered instructions still follow sequence.
- Now, currently, recently: Keep words like “now”, “currently”, “recently”, “last year” as written; resolve only what the response itself dates.
- A comparison: Keep the comparison with the baseline the response gives, inside the claim. Without one, keep the comparison as stated; never add a baseline from elsewhere.
- A rank: Keep a rank (superlative, ordinal, “top ten”) with its class. Never drop the class or add one. “The best”, “the most important” are judgements, not ranks.
- Words left out: Supply the left-out words from the same sentence, in its words; add nothing else.
- A bare or polar answer: A bare phrase or a polar word that only the user's question would complete (“About 11 months.”, “Yes.”, “No.”) gives no claim here: you do not see the question. Before a full sentence that says the same, it adds nothing; extract the sentence. A sentence whose subject only the question names (“It lasts about 11 months.”) keeps that subject as written.
- Here and the nearest place: Resolve “here” and the viewpoint of “nearest” from the response’s own named place. If no place is given, retain the readable location claim with “here” as written; do not drop it or supply a place from elsewhere. Keep the stated distance and direction together.

Identity and equivalence of expressions
- What a word stands for or means: A definition in the main clause (“APR stands for …”, “APR means …”) is a claim about the word, in the response's own verb and with its own hedge (“could stand for”). An expansion given in passing (“APR, short for …”) is an alias inside the claim it identifies.
- A second name for the same thing: Keep both names inside the one claim, as written: (the World Health Organization (WHO) | recommends …). No claim for the name, no expansion the response did not give. A main-clause “X stands for Y” is a definition. Spelling variants, missing accents and transliterations of the same name remain in the response’s spelling and identify one entity; no extra equivalence claim is added. Similar spelling is not enough when the names identify different entities, and an ambiguous name is not resolved from outside knowledge.
- Same value in two units: One value is one claim, in both units, as written. Supply an omitted unit only from the response’s own heading or sentence. Otherwise retain the readable unitless claim as written; never drop it, invent a unit, or guess from the number. A dimensionless count needs no physical unit.
- Numbers in words: Keep numbers as written, in any notation: “12”, “twelve”, “a dozen”. A number word with a fixed value is that value (“a baker's dozen” is 13). Vague numerals (“a few”, “several”, “dozens”) are quantities, read by their usual span.
- Percentages, fractions and their base: Keep shares as written, with their base inside, and a change as one claim with both values and the date: (a quarter of registered voters | turned out, up from | one in five in 2019). Percent and percentage points are kept apart.
- Dates, times and time zones: Keep dates, times and time zones as written; never convert. A period (“spring 2027”, “the 1990s”) is kept as a period.
- An amount in another currency: Do not extract an amount converted into another currency; keep the amount in the currency the response states it in. The same currency in another notation is the same amount.
- The same statement in another form: Extract in the response's own words; do not rewrite into a canonical direction, voice or polarity. A negative word stays where the response writes it. The one fixed form is the imperative's, which has no claim form of its own.

Tense, aspect and change over time
- A value that changed: One claim holds the change, in the response's own words: both values, the direction and the date. Never fragments, and never the old value as the current one. A reported change states its result: the new value holds at the text's own time, unless the text says it changed again.
- Tense: Keep tense, aspect and forecast markers as written (was, is, will, is expected to, has been, used to); never turn a past into a present or a forecast into a fact. An unscheduled prediction is extracted too, with its own future time and certainty. Never turn “will likely” into a present fact or discard it because the future is unknown.
- Steps in order: Each step is a claim, and a step that depends on another keeps its order to the next step inside, in the response's own order words (first, then, finally, before): (you | should sand the fence first, then prime | the fence). Steps the response gives in no particular order get no order. Advice takes the advice form, (you | should … | …).

Discourse structure
- A conclusion the response draws: Extract the conclusion as the response states it, with its own hedge, and the premises as facts. A conclusion introduced by a premise (“This suggests X”, “…, implying X”, “…, indicating X”) is the response’s own: the conclusion in the fixed form (that X | is | suggested), with its own hedge words inside X; the premise is not its subject, and neither is a passage. Never a claim about the reasoning itself (“X implies Y”).
- A label with a value, or a sentence cut off: A label with its value has no claim form of its own, so it takes one fixed form: the heading and the label, the value, joined by “is”, in the list's own words: (recommended sleep per night for adults | is | 7 to 9 hours). An unfinished sentence gives nothing beyond its complete part. Every claim must read alone as subject, relation and object.
- The same fact twice: Two statements are one claim only if no text could judge them differently: equivalent content, the same commitment, the same strength. A hedged and a plain version, a sourced and a plain version, a summary that generalises, are separate claims. A passage is no source in this sense: “Passage 4 notes that X” and “X” are one claim.
- Lists, headings and tables: A heading, a bullet or a table is a frame, not a claim: every item and every cell carries the headings and headers that identify it. A labelled item takes the one fixed form a label has (heading + label | is | value); a table cell whose column header is a verb (“Opens”) keeps it as the verb. A listing whose heading or lead-in names the set (“Opening hours”, “Track listing”, “Cast”, “the five members are”) is complete: a day, track or member without an entry is not one, and a property given in a fixed slot of such a listing (a column, or a bracketed form the listing uses for it) is stated for each entry, so an empty slot states its absence. “Selected”, “some” and “include” leave the set open, a list in running text states nothing by its silence, and a listing that is visibly cut off (it ends mid-entry or with an ellipsis) closes nothing.
- An answer in parts for different readings: Each part's claims carry the reading or audience that fixes them, inside the claim: (a bass (the fish) | is | …). The part label is a frame, not a condition and not a claim.
- A written calculation: Each displayed equality is one claim, keeping its operands, operations, units and identifying label in the response’s notation; the written relation (such as “=”) is its predicate. In a chain, take each adjacent equality, carrying the label into each. A result given alone uses the label-with-value form. Extract separately stated input facts too, but never invent omitted steps or restate a displayed result as another claim.

Examples (invented):
- "Based on the passages, ginger may ease nausea and bloating (Passage 3). The passages do not say whether it helps with migraines." -> (ginger | may ease | nausea), (ginger | may ease | bloating)
- "Critics argue that the new tram line, opened in 2021, is too slow." -> (critics | argue that | the new tram line is too slow), (the new tram line | opened in | 2021)
- "Studies suggest that walking after meals lowers blood sugar." -> (studies | suggest that | walking after meals lowers blood sugar)
- "You can get a refund if you return the jacket within 14 days." -> (you | can get a refund if | you return the jacket within 14 days)
- "In 2019 the city raised the parking fee from $2 to $3 an hour." -> (the city | raised the parking fee in 2019 from $2 to | $3 an hour)
- "The museum does not open on Mondays, but it opens late on Fridays." -> (the museum | does not open on | Mondays), (the museum | opens late on | Fridays)
- "Do not store the paint below 5 °C. I hope this helps!" -> (you | should not store | the paint below 5 °C)
- "Passage 2 suggests that the ferry runs in winter, while Passage 5 says it stops in October." -> (that the ferry runs in winter | is | suggested), (that the ferry stops in October | is | stated)

Return JSON with a triplets array.

If the response makes no claim about the world (it only abstains, frames or asks), return an empty triplets array.

extractor_prompt_plain.instructions:
Extract every claim the response below makes, as triplets: (subject | predicate | object).

Basic rules:
- A claim is one triplet. Extract every claim the response makes, right or wrong; never correct, repair or complete it.

The situations below decide everything else. Each line is one rule.

Assertion, presupposition and speech act
- Talk about the text or the answer itself: A sentence about the response itself, not about the topic, gives no claim: words that organise the text (“here is the answer”, “in summary”, “key points”), a frame that names the response's source (“based on the information provided”), what the response, its sources or its author is or is not (“I am an AI assistant”, “this may not be accurate”, “this is not medical advice”, “the passages focus mainly on …”), and a sign-off (“I hope this helps”). Remarks to or about the user or the conversation (“you may be thinking of …”, “I apologize for my mistake”) give no claim either. A stance of the sources against content (“other passages express skepticism about X”) is not such talk: it gives (X | is | doubted). The content such a frame introduces is extracted as usual. A source frame drops only when the content after it is about the world; when it is about evidence or knowledge (“based on the passages, there is no clear evidence that …”, “… it is unclear whether …”), the sentence says what the passages lack and gives no claim. Advice to the reader stays advice even when it is about the answer (“do not rely on this alone”). A disclaimer about the whole answer does not weaken the claims around it. Pure emphasis (“of course”, “obviously”, “naturally”, “indeed”) is dropped; a word that says how the speaker knows (“evidently”, “apparently”) or how sure they are (“definitely”, “probably”) stays in the claim.
- A question in the response: A question gives no claim, whatever it is for, including an offer to the reader (“Would you like more details?”) and a rhetorical question. The response's answer to its own question is extracted as stated, read with that question: “Do cats purr only when happy? No: …” gives (cats | do not purr only when | they are happy).
- Assumed background: What a sentence only takes for granted is not a claim of its own, unless the response adds new information there (a date, a name, a number): “the ban they imposed in 2019” gives (the commissioners | imposed the burn ban in | 2019). A factive verb (“know that”, “discovered that”, “realised that”) takes its complement as true: the complement is a claim of its own, next to the claim about the holder: “Residents know that the vote is on Monday” gives (residents | know that | the vote is on Monday) and (the vote | is on | Monday). A non-factive verb (“believe that”, “claim that”) does not. A source with a reporting verb that passes its content on as fact (“tests show that”) stays one claim.
- What the wording suggests: Extract what the response says, not what its wording suggests. A limit it states outright (“only some”, “not all”, “no other”) is part of the claim. One named exception: a threshold or condition stated as a rule is the rule.
- Vague statements about the world: A statement about the world is a claim even when it is vague, and even when it is about what is known (“more research is needed”, “experts disagree”). A sentence that announces a list but says something about the topic (“there are several factors to consider:”) is a claim; one that only points at the text (“here are the factors:”) is not. Content passed on from the sources is the response’s own claim: “the sources describe several uses of borax” gives (borax | has | several uses).
- An abstention: A sentence that says the response or its passages leave something open gives no claim, whether it covers part of the question or all of it: what the passages or the information given lack (“the passages do not say whether …”, “there is no information on …”, “the passages conflict”, “the evidence does not clearly indicate whether …” when the evidence is the material the response was given), what the response cannot settle itself (“I do not know whether …”, “the evidence in the passages is mixed, so it is hard to say”), or what would settle it (“more information would help draw a firmer conclusion”, “more data would be needed to be sure”). Everything else in the response is extracted. Doubt about the world with nothing that points at the response is a claim: (whether hedgehogs eat snails | is | unclear); “more research is needed”; “experts disagree”.
- A judgement: A judgement is a claim, in the response's own strength. A judgement inside a noun phrase (“the vital canal”) is split off as its own claim, and the host claim is stated without it. An exclamation is classified by what it says, not by its punctuation: a judgement about the topic is a claim, while praise of the response itself follows filler. A sentence adverb that judges its whole event (“unfortunately”, “surprisingly”) becomes a judgement of that event, using the adverb’s adjective form and the event’s own words; the event is extracted without it. Do not invent “I think” or a new holder. The judgement is not supported merely because the event is.
- Advice and instructions: An imperative is the one sentence with no claim form of its own, so it takes one fixed form: its understood subject “you” and “should”, every other word as written: (you | should seal | your grout once a year), (you | should never use | bleach on coloured grout). A sentence with its own subject keeps it as written, with its own strength word: (grout | can be sealed | once a year), (you | can reduce your heating bill by | insulating the loft). A caveat or disclaimer is advice too and takes the same form: “As always, consult your doctor or pharmacist” gives (you | should consult | your doctor or pharmacist). A sentence about the answer itself (“this is not medical advice”) gives no claim; advice about what to do with the answer (“do not rely on this alone”) is advice like any other. A first-person recommendation (“I recommend that you …”, “I suggest …”, “I advise …”) keeps its own words and counts as advice at “should” strength: (I | recommend that you seal | your grout once a year). Generic “one” in reader advice keeps that subject and its written strength; “one should” is advice to the reader, and “you must” is an obligation. In an answer about what to do, “can” is advice at its weakest strength (“grout can be sealed once a year”); a “can” that states what something is able to do is “Ability, permission and obligation”, and “may” as possibility is hedge.
- An imagined case or worked example: An imagined case is one conditional claim, its assumption inside: (a car bought for $30,000 | would be worth after a year | about $25,000). Its invented premise is never a claim of its own. A counterfactual (“had …, would have …”) is also one conditional claim: keep its condition and consequence together. Do not add the condition’s negation as an actual event merely because the wording suggests it; an actual event stated separately is extracted separately.
- A response that contradicts itself: Extract every assertion as stated, right or wrong, never repaired. A statement the response itself takes back is not asserted.
- Code, formulas and commands: Keep each written formula as one complete relation and each code listing as one text value under its supplied heading or surrounding prose. A recommended command uses the advice form, (you | should … | …), and retains flags and arguments. A block without a heading is still extracted; do not turn a listing into invented claims about execution or results.
- An ironic statement: When the response’s own words make irony unmistakable, the literal ironic judgement gives no claim; keep every separately asserted fact or judgement in its own words. Do not invent the opposite as a claim. Without an unmistakable cue, take praise at its word, even if it seems unlikely.
- A figure of speech: Keep a metaphor, idiom or clear hyperbole in the response’s own words as one assertion, including the words that identify its subject and scope. Do not replace the expression with an extractor-invented paraphrase, or discard it as non-factual. Actual measurements stay literal; where wording leaves the meaning unclear, do not invent a precise interpretation.
- Output not composed as an answer: Text that is not composed as an answer gives no claim: an echo of the question, a page label, site name or headline, a song line or other quoted line that says nothing about the world, and stray tokens. A declarative sentence about the world is a claim wherever it stands, however broken the text around it; a statement repeated in a loop is one claim, and an unfinished one gives nothing beyond its complete part. A response is never dropped whole for being degenerate.
- Content composed on request: A poem, story, rewritten lyrics or sample dialogue the response composes, on request or labelled as its own (“here is my version”), is not put forward as information and gives no claim. Lines the response presents as an existing work’s text are a quotation claim about that work: (Harbour Lights | opens with the lines | “…”). A statement about the work outside the composition (its author, its year) is a claim as usual.
- “Managed to” and “failed to”: Keep an implicative verb as written: (the Kestrel expedition | managed to reach | the summit of Mount Arden). It states its result: “managed to X” and “succeeded in X-ing” state X, “failed to X” states that X did not happen. The effort or attempt the verb takes for granted is not a claim of its own: it stays inside the verb, which the claim keeps, and is not checked. A verb that only reports an attempt or a wish (“tried to”, “hoped to”, “planned to”) states nothing about the result.

Evidentiality and attribution
- Someone else's view: Someone else's view keeps its holder: (holder | says / argues / believes | the whole view). A fact said in passing is the response's own plain claim. A second holder around the first frames the whole: (the local paper | reports that | critics expect …). A vague or collective holder (“experts”, “it is widely believed”) stays exactly as written, with any agreement or frequency word inside the reported claim. “Experts agree that X” is one attributed claim, not an extra claim that a consensus exists. An explicit agreement is stronger than merely reporting that some people hold the view; do not erase that distinction. “Studies show” follows “How strongly a reporting verb puts its content” rather than being flattened into a belief. A named holder (a named person, organisation, publication or dated study) stays as written like any other holder.
- References to the passages: Nothing that points to the material the response was given is part of a claim: no passage number, citation marker, count of passages (“most passages”) or noun for that material (“the passages”, “the evidence”, “the information” when it means the material). By default the response passes the content on as its own: “Passage 4 notes that X”, “the information lists X” and “X (Passage 2)” all give the plain claim X. Where the response keeps its distance, the content takes a fixed form without the source: content put as only suggested (“Passage 4 suggests X”, and “the evidence indicates X” or “the information indicates X” summing up the material, the response’s own inference; one passage that “indicates X” passes X on) gives (that X | is | suggested); content the response marks as not adopted (it sets it against contrary content, or calls it doubtful or someone’s claim) gives (that X | is | stated); a stance of the material against content (“other passages express skepticism about X”) gives (X | is | doubted), without “that” before a noun phrase. When the response reports passages that disagree, each side is its own claim in these forms. A judgement about a source gives a claim only if it states or hedges a statement about the world: “the figure of 27 appears outdated” gives (the Air Force enlistment age figure of 27 | appears | outdated), with “the figure” resolved from the response, while “Passage 3 is unclear” gives none; a report that the matter is open (“the passages conflict on X”) gives no claim. “Suggests” meaning “recommends” takes the advice form. A URL used only as a citation marker drops with that marker. A statement locating information at a named resource (“fees are listed at …”) is an ordinary claim and keeps the address as written; an instruction to visit it follows instruction. A bare link takes a supplied label, never an invented description of what the page contains.
- How strongly a reporting verb puts its content: Keep a reporting verb as written, with its source: (research | suggests that | houseplants take some pollutants out of indoor air). The verb sets the strength: “show”, “find”, “confirm” pass the content on as fact; “suggest”, “imply”, “point to” make it only possible; “indicate” passes the content on when its subject is a text (a report, an article, a passage) and makes it only possible when its subject is evidence or data; “say”, “argue”, “claim” report a view (attribution). Never rewrite the verb into a hedge, never drop it. When the source is the material the response was given, nothing that points to it stays: “Passage 2 states X” and “Passage 2 indicates X” give the plain claim X; “Passage 1 suggests X”, and “the evidence indicates X” or “the information indicates X” summing up the material, give (that X | is | suggested).
- “Allegedly”, “reportedly”, “apparently”: Keep the evidential adverb as written, in the predicate: (the mayor | allegedly accepted | gifts from a developer). “Allegedly” and “reportedly” mark someone else's statement; “apparently” and “evidently” say what the evidence shows.
- Quotations: Keep quotation marks where the response puts them. A person's words are their statement, (person | says / calls / describes … as | “content”), judged as their view. A quoted passage given as evidence is the response's own plain claim (the passage goes). Words in scare quotes stay inside the claim they stand in, as someone else's term: (the “miracle cure” diet | helped participants … lose | …).

Modality, quantity and precision
- Uncertainty: Keep the hedge at its strength, in the predicate, and copy it into every item it governs. Never add one and never drop one. A first-person “I think”, “I believe” or “I suspect” is a hedge on its clause: keep it as written, with the author as subject, (I | think that | X), read as the author’s own X at about the strength of “probably”; in front of a list it governs every item. “I know X” is a plain assertion.
- An approximate number: Keep the approximation word with its number. “About X” covers X plus or minus the larger of 10% and half the step of X's last non-zero digit; an exact number covers what rounds to it. Keep an explicit margin with its central value and unit; an unqualified “X ± d” gives those written bounds, not the default “about” tolerance. Keep a named confidence interval and its confidence level inside the statistical estimate. A confidence interval is not a spread of individual observations or a guarantee that the true value lies inside; a bare point estimate does not establish a reported confidence interval.
- A range: A range is one claim, as written. A plain range says the value lies somewhere in it; “ranges from”, “varies from”, “as little as” also claim that the ends occur.
- A bound: Keep the bound word with the number, as written. “Over” and “more than” exclude the number; “at least” and “or older” include it.
- How many, how often: Keep the quantifier or frequency word at its strength, in the subject or the predicate. Never add one and never drop one. Keep generic “people” and “one” as written too: an explicit “often” or “always” remains part of that claim, not a universal subject or advice. In a statement about service availability, retain that scope rather than turning it into a claim about how frequently each person acts. A vague numeral is a quantifier too, read by its usual span: a couple 2, a few 3 to 5, several 3 to 7, dozens 24 or more; it is never normalised to a number.
- A bare plural: Keep a bare plural bare and read it as a generic about the kind: it allows exceptions. It is found in “most”, “usually”, “typically”, “generally”; not in “some”, “many” or “a few”. One named exception: a generic about a danger (carries a disease, bites, stings, is poisonous) says only that members can have it, and is found in “some” or “a few”.
- A degree word: Keep the degree word where it modifies. Never add one and never drop one.
- A statistical value: Keep the response’s name for the statistic with its value, outcome, population and any stated comparison. Do not turn a summary into an individual value, equate risk with odds, or invent an absolute rate. A relative-risk statement remains a claim without a numerical baseline or named comparison group; keep its stated scope and never fill the omission.
- Ability, permission and obligation: Keep the response's modal and its meaning: capacity (“can lift”), permission (“are permitted to”) and an obligation on someone other than the reader (“applicants must be residents”) stay distinct from each other and are never turned into an asserted occurrence. A possibility (“may”, “might”, “could” meaning possibly) is a hedge, with its own scale (Uncertainty). Reader advice (“you should”, “you must register”) is advice (Advice and instructions).

Negation, polarity and exclusion
- A negation: Keep the negation as written, where the response puts it, with its scope words: “will not directly kill”, “kills none of them directly”, “nobody under 18 may apply”. Never move it, never reword it. Carry it into every item it covers: under “not”, “A or B” gives one negative claim per item. Keep “not uncommon”, “not impossible” and “not without” intact; do not strengthen them into an unqualified positive. Keep negation and its quantifier in their written order: “not every” is not “none”. If “all … not” remains ambiguous, preserve the full wording rather than choosing a reading. A “not X but Y” correction states the negative and the positive as separate claims, with their shared subject and verb restored from the sentence; an explicit retraction follows “A response that contradicts itself”.
- An exception: Keep the exception inside the one claim. Never split the rule from its exception: the rule alone overgeneralises.
- “Only”: Keep “only”, “just”, “solely” where they stand, inside the claim. Never add one and never drop one. A cleft (“It is electric trains that …”) keeps its focus as written; its “no one else” is an implicature, not part of the claim, unless “only” is said.
- “Need not”, “must not”, “may not”: Keep the response's own modal and negation words in their order (“need not”, “must not”, “may not”, “cannot”); do not reword them to settle their meaning.

Coordination and plurality
- List of items: One claim per item. Keep the items together when they only work together (a mix, a pair, “both”), and when they name the members of a definite plural (“the X are A and B”, a bare list answering “which X …”): that claim says these are all, so one wrong or missing member sinks it.
- Items that only hold together: Do not split items that only hold together: a shared value, a sum, a blend, a comparison or relation between the items, a pair (“both”). Test: read each part alone; split only if it says what the response says, with nothing lost and nothing that held only for the items together.
- Alternatives (A or B): Keep “A or B” whole, except under an operator that makes it apply to each item: a negation (not, never, no, without), the condition of an “if”, or a permission (can, may: “you may bring a laptop or a tablet” allows each). There, one claim per item, each with the operator. First ask whether the “or” gives a second name (alias) or one definition.
- A class with examples: One claim per example, the class inside: (the stall | sells | dried fruits such as figs). No membership claims, unless membership is what the sentence says (“examples of aggravated DUI include repeat offences”). “Some examples include” is not a hedge.
- Paired lists: Pair the items in order, one claim per pair. Never the cross product of the two lists.
- An open list (“etc.”): “Etc.”, “and more”, “among others” are not items: split the list, one claim per named item. A list made complete (“the only things”, “just these three”) is one claim with its “only”.

Modification and subordination
- A detail that adds a fact: A detail that adds a fact (an apposition, a non-restrictive relative clause, a parenthesis, a title before a name) is a claim of its own, the thing named in full; the host claim is stated without it. Test: without it, the claim is about the same thing and still true.
- A detail that says which thing is meant: Keep a restriction inside the one claim: (trains with diesel engines | are banned from | the tunnel). Test: without it, would the claim be about other things or say more? A detail that only adds a fact about things already identified is split off. A modifier that could belong to either of two nouns (“trains carrying lorries with diesel engines”) stays inside the complete phrase as written; it is resolved only when the response’s own wording fixes it, never from outside knowledge. An adjective that says the thing is not, or is no longer, what the noun names (“former”, “fake”, “toy”, “imitation”) is not a restriction: it names something else, so former diesel trains are not a narrower group of diesel trains. Keep it as written, inside the claim.
- A condition: Keep the condition inside the one claim (if, when, once, unless, depending on, a deadline with “by”). Never the bare statement plus a separate condition claim. “Even if” is no condition: “q even if p” asserts q in every case, p included, so the clause stays inside the one claim, (q | even if | p), and p itself is not a claim.
- What an action is for: Split a purpose off as its own claim, in the response's own words, every reference resolved: “it works best that way” gives (the fertilizer | works best | spread when the weather is dry). The advice is stated without it, in the advice form, (you | should … | …). Drop test: without the purpose, is the advice still true as meant? If not, the purpose is a condition of the advice and stays inside: (you | should return | unopened bags within 30 days to get a refund). Under a negation or prohibition the purpose stays inside too.
- Cause and effect: Attach each effect to the cause the response names; never a chain the response does not state, never reversed. A chain the response states gives one claim per stated link. Events joined by a bare “so” or “therefore” are each a claim, but the link between them states no cause. A reason that is a fact of its own is its own claim. Weaker causal words (“linked to”, “may contribute to”) stay as written.
- “Although”, “but”: One claim per clause; the contrast word (although, but, while, however) gives no claim.
- By what means, in what manner: Keep the means, instrument or manner inside the claim it modifies, in the response's own words. A sentence with its own subject keeps it, a generic “you” included: (you | can reduce your heating bill by | insulating the loft). Only an imperative, which has no subject, takes the advice form, (you | should … | …).

Reference, deixis and context dependence
- A word that points to something: Resolve every reference from the response itself; add nothing from the world. Name a sense, with the response's own head noun, only where the response gives the word two senses. A reference the response never resolves stays as written.
- A frame: place, day, heading: Copy a place, date, product or heading set once into every claim it governs, in the fixed form a label with its value takes: (the forecast for Ashby on Saturday | is | dry and sunny). The frame is part of the claim; it is never a claim of its own. A stated relation between events (“after the merger”, “before the opening”) is a time frame kept inside the event it locates. A separately asserted event is extracted separately, but the time phrase alone is not split into an extra occurrence claim or a causal link. Ordered instructions still follow sequence.
- Now, currently, recently: Keep words like “now”, “currently”, “recently”, “last year” as written; resolve only what the response itself dates.
- A comparison: Keep the comparison with the baseline the response gives, inside the claim. Without one, keep the comparison as stated; never add a baseline from elsewhere.
- A rank: Keep a rank (superlative, ordinal, “top ten”) with its class. Never drop the class or add one. “The best”, “the most important” are judgements, not ranks.
- Words left out: Supply the left-out words from the same sentence, in its words; add nothing else.
- A bare or polar answer: A bare phrase or a polar word that only the user's question would complete (“About 11 months.”, “Yes.”, “No.”) gives no claim here: you do not see the question. Before a full sentence that says the same, it adds nothing; extract the sentence. A sentence whose subject only the question names (“It lasts about 11 months.”) keeps that subject as written.
- Here and the nearest place: Resolve “here” and the viewpoint of “nearest” from the response’s own named place. If no place is given, retain the readable location claim with “here” as written; do not drop it or supply a place from elsewhere. Keep the stated distance and direction together.

Identity and equivalence of expressions
- What a word stands for or means: A definition in the main clause (“APR stands for …”, “APR means …”) is a claim about the word, in the response's own verb and with its own hedge (“could stand for”). An expansion given in passing (“APR, short for …”) is an alias inside the claim it identifies.
- A second name for the same thing: Keep both names inside the one claim, as written: (the World Health Organization (WHO) | recommends …). No claim for the name, no expansion the response did not give. A main-clause “X stands for Y” is a definition. Spelling variants, missing accents and transliterations of the same name remain in the response’s spelling and identify one entity; no extra equivalence claim is added. Similar spelling is not enough when the names identify different entities, and an ambiguous name is not resolved from outside knowledge.
- Same value in two units: One value is one claim, in both units, as written. Supply an omitted unit only from the response’s own heading or sentence. Otherwise retain the readable unitless claim as written; never drop it, invent a unit, or guess from the number. A dimensionless count needs no physical unit.
- Numbers in words: Keep numbers as written, in any notation: “12”, “twelve”, “a dozen”. A number word with a fixed value is that value (“a baker's dozen” is 13). Vague numerals (“a few”, “several”, “dozens”) are quantities, read by their usual span.
- Percentages, fractions and their base: Keep shares as written, with their base inside, and a change as one claim with both values and the date: (a quarter of registered voters | turned out, up from | one in five in 2019). Percent and percentage points are kept apart.
- Dates, times and time zones: Keep dates, times and time zones as written; never convert. A period (“spring 2027”, “the 1990s”) is kept as a period.
- An amount in another currency: Do not extract an amount converted into another currency; keep the amount in the currency the response states it in. The same currency in another notation is the same amount.
- The same statement in another form: Extract in the response's own words; do not rewrite into a canonical direction, voice or polarity. A negative word stays where the response writes it. The one fixed form is the imperative's, which has no claim form of its own.

Tense, aspect and change over time
- A value that changed: One claim holds the change, in the response's own words: both values, the direction and the date. Never fragments, and never the old value as the current one. A reported change states its result: the new value holds at the text's own time, unless the text says it changed again.
- Tense: Keep tense, aspect and forecast markers as written (was, is, will, is expected to, has been, used to); never turn a past into a present or a forecast into a fact. An unscheduled prediction is extracted too, with its own future time and certainty. Never turn “will likely” into a present fact or discard it because the future is unknown.
- Steps in order: Each step is a claim, and a step that depends on another keeps its order to the next step inside, in the response's own order words (first, then, finally, before): (you | should sand the fence first, then prime | the fence). Steps the response gives in no particular order get no order. Advice takes the advice form, (you | should … | …).

Discourse structure
- A conclusion the response draws: Extract the conclusion as the response states it, with its own hedge, and the premises as facts. A conclusion introduced by a premise (“This suggests X”, “…, implying X”, “…, indicating X”) is the response’s own: the conclusion in the fixed form (that X | is | suggested), with its own hedge words inside X; the premise is not its subject, and neither is a passage. Never a claim about the reasoning itself (“X implies Y”).
- A label with a value, or a sentence cut off: A label with its value has no claim form of its own, so it takes one fixed form: the heading and the label, the value, joined by “is”, in the list's own words: (recommended sleep per night for adults | is | 7 to 9 hours). An unfinished sentence gives nothing beyond its complete part. Every claim must read alone as subject, relation and object.
- The same fact twice: Two statements are one claim only if no text could judge them differently: equivalent content, the same commitment, the same strength. A hedged and a plain version, a sourced and a plain version, a summary that generalises, are separate claims. A passage is no source in this sense: “Passage 4 notes that X” and “X” are one claim.
- Lists, headings and tables: A heading, a bullet or a table is a frame, not a claim: every item and every cell carries the headings and headers that identify it. A labelled item takes the one fixed form a label has (heading + label | is | value); a table cell whose column header is a verb (“Opens”) keeps it as the verb. A listing whose heading or lead-in names the set (“Opening hours”, “Track listing”, “Cast”, “the five members are”) is complete: a day, track or member without an entry is not one, and a property given in a fixed slot of such a listing (a column, or a bracketed form the listing uses for it) is stated for each entry, so an empty slot states its absence. “Selected”, “some” and “include” leave the set open, a list in running text states nothing by its silence, and a listing that is visibly cut off (it ends mid-entry or with an ellipsis) closes nothing.
- An answer in parts for different readings: Each part's claims carry the reading or audience that fixes them, inside the claim: (a bass (the fish) | is | …). The part label is a frame, not a condition and not a claim.
- A written calculation: Each displayed equality is one claim, keeping its operands, operations, units and identifying label in the response’s notation; the written relation (such as “=”) is its predicate. In a chain, take each adjacent equality, carrying the label into each. A result given alone uses the label-with-value form. Extract separately stated input facts too, but never invent omitted steps or restate a displayed result as another claim.

claim_match_prompt.system: You are a factual entailment judge.
claim_match_prompt.instructions:
You are evaluating the semantic equivalence of knowledge graph triplets extracted from a text.
Your task is to check if a predicted triplet (the Claim) is semantically entailed by a list of ground truth triplets (the Reference).
Each claim is numbered with an ID in brackets, like [1]. Reference triplets are labelled separately as (R1), (R2), ... — an (R) label is never a claim id.

IMPORTANT RULES FOR SEMANTIC EQUIVALENCE:
1. Subject-Object Reversal: Triplets that swap the subject and object but maintain the same meaning are matching. For example, '(the landslide, was caused by, heavy rainfall)' is structurally different but semantically IDENTICAL to '(heavy rainfall, caused, the landslide)'. Mark as Entailment.
2. Split/Merge: A claim that names fewer items than the reference is entailed by it: '(the powder, kills, ants)' is entailed by '(the powder, kills, ants, roaches and fleas)'. Items the reference states separately entail a claim that joins them with 'and'. A claim that names all the members of a set says these are all: '(the founders of the band, were, Ada and Ben)' is entailed only by a reference that gives exactly these members as the set, NOT by '(the founders of the band, included, Ada and Ben)'. 'Or' is not a list of facts: '(your bag, must fit in, the overhead bin)' is NOT entailed by '(your bag, must fit in, the overhead bin or under the seat)'. Under a negation or a permission, 'or' applies to each item: '(you, may bring, a tablet)' is entailed by '(you, may bring, a laptop or a tablet)', and '(you, must never pack, lighters)' by '(you, must never pack, batteries or lighters)'. Items that only hold together (a shared value, a sum, a mixture, a comparison between the items, a pair) are one fact: '(the renewal, costs, a $50 processing fee)' plus '(the renewal, costs, a $50 shipping fee)' is NOT entailed by '(the renewal, costs, one $50 fee for processing and shipping)'; '(the renewal, costs, a $50 fee)' is. Mark as Neutral where it is not entailed.
3. Paraphrasing: Treat synonyms and paraphrased phrases as matching if the core factual meaning is the same. The forms of one name match ('NASA' and 'the National Aeronautics and Space Administration', a spelling without accents); a second name that only a fact gives (a birth name, a stage name, a former name) does not.
4. Certainty: How certain a triplet is belongs to its meaning, and it works one way. A claim that is less certain than the reference is entailed by it; a claim that is more certain is not. '(the ferry, may stop running in, winter)' IS entailed by '(the ferry, stops running in, winter)'; '(the ferry, stops running in, winter)' is NOT entailed by '(the ferry, may stop running in, winter)'. Mark as Neutral. Hedges of the same strength still match ('may' and 'might'). A view given to a generic holder ('some critics', 'studies', 'experts') says less than the plain fact: '(some critics, believe, the film is too long)' IS entailed by '(the film, is, too long)', because a generic holder is read, not checked; '(the film, is, too long)' is NOT entailed by '(some critics, believe, the film is too long)'. A named holder (a named person, organisation, publication or dated study) is a fact of its own: '(the Harbour Times, reports that, the film is too long)' is NOT entailed by '(the film, is, too long)'. Precision works the same way: '(the bridge, is, about 350 metres long)' is entailed by '(the bridge, is, 340 metres long)'; '(the bridge, is, 340 metres long)' is NOT entailed by '(the bridge, is, about 350 metres long)'.
5. Polarity: A negation or an opposite assessment is never a match, even on the same topic. '(the tea, may help with, insomnia)' and '(the tea, has insufficient evidence for helping with, insomnia)' say opposite things. Never mark them as Entailment.
6. Source: Nothing that points to the material the response was given is part of a claim: a passage number, a citation marker, or 'the passages', 'the evidence', 'the information' when they mean that material. A passage that passes a fact on, whatever the verb ('states', 'notes', 'says', 'confirms', and 'indicates' with a passage as subject), is not part of the claim: '(Passage 3, states, the dam is 40 metres high)' and '(the dam, is, 40 metres high)' are the same claim. Mark as Entailment. Content the response only suggests, reports without adopting, or sees its material doubt takes the forms '(that X, is, suggested)', '(that X, is, stated)', '(X, is, doubted)'; a triplet that still names the material as the subject of such a verb is read in that form ('(Passage 3, suggests that, X)' is '(that X, is, suggested)'). A form matches the same form; the plain X is NOT entailed by any of them. Mark as Neutral.
7. Strength: Words that set how strong or how wide a claim is belong to its meaning, as hedges do: 'should', 'must'; 'all', 'most', 'many', 'some'; 'only'; 'greatly', 'modestly'; 'shows' versus 'suggests'. A claim that says less, or says it less strongly, is entailed by a reference that says more; a claim that says more is NOT entailed by a reference that says less. '(many banks, notarize for free, documents of customers)' IS entailed by '(most banks, notarize for free, documents of customers)'; '(all banks, notarize for free, documents of customers)' is NOT. '(studies, suggest that, X)' IS entailed by '(studies, show that, X)'; '(studies, show that, X)' is NOT entailed by '(studies, suggest that, X)'. A claim without 'only' or a degree word is entailed by one with it, not the other way round. Mark as Neutral where it is not entailed. The same strength in other words still matches ('must' and 'have to').
8. Holder: A view given to a different holder is a different claim. '(critics, argue that, the stadium will raise rents)' is NOT the same as '(supporters, argue that, the stadium will raise rents)'. Mark as Neutral. The same kind of holder in other words still matches ('studies' and 'research').
9. Conditions and thresholds: A condition, a threshold or a bound is part of the claim. '(the fee, is, deductible)' is NOT entailed by '(the fee, is deductible if, expenses exceed 7.5% of income)', and '(applicants, must be, over 18)' is NOT entailed by '(applicants, must be, at least 18)'. Mark as Neutral. A claim that only says something may be possible keeps matching without the condition: '(the fee, may be, deductible)' IS entailed by '(the fee, is deductible if, expenses exceed 7.5% of income)'.
10. Same value, other form: The same value written another way matches: units ('3.4 kg' and '7.5 lb'), number words ('a dozen' and '12'), shares ('25%' and 'a quarter'), date notation ('30 March 2027' and 'March 30, 2027'). Mark as Entailment.
11. Changes: A change states its result. '(the city, raised the fee in 2019 from $2 to, $3)' entails '(the fee, is, $3)'; it does NOT entail '(the fee, is, $2)'.
12. A claim that names nothing: A claim whose subject only points ('it', 'they', 'this', 'the second group') and names nothing is NOT entailed by a claim that names the thing, and the other claims never fill it in. '(it, opened in, 1931)' is NOT entailed by '(the station, opened in, 1931)'. Mark as Neutral.

If the Claim is supported by ANY triplet in the Reference, answer 'Entailment'.
If NO triplet in the Reference entails the Claim, and it is contradicted, answer 'Contradiction'.
Otherwise, answer 'Neutral'.

For EACH claim, first explain your reasoning step by step in the 'explanation' field, then give your verdict. Return the claim_id (the number in brackets), your explanation, and the verdict for every claim. Do NOT skip any claim. Do NOT return the claim text.

says less, or says it less strongly, matches a reference that says more ('may stop' matches
'stops'; 'some critics believe X' matches 'X'; 'suggests' matches 'shows'; 'many' matches
'most'; 'about 350 m' matches '340 m'; 'may be deductible' matches 'deductible if over 7.5%').
The forms of one name match ('NASA' and its full name). Nothing that points to the given material is part of the
claim ('Passage 3 states X' and 'Passage 3 indicates X' match 'X'; 'Passage 3 suggests X' matches
'(that X, is, suggested)', not 'X').

It is NOT a match when the claim says more, or says it more strongly, than the reference
('stops' against 'may stop', 'X' against 'some critics believe X', 'shows' against 'suggests',
'all' against 'most', '340 m' against 'about 350 m', 'only' or a degree word added), when it
negates or reverses the reference, when it takes one alternative out of an 'or' ('must fit in
the bin' against 'must fit in the bin or under the seat'; under a negation or a permission each

'supporters'), or when it drops a condition or changes a threshold ('deductible' against
'deductible if over 7.5%', 'over 18' against 'at least 18'). Items that only hold together
('one $50 fee for processing and shipping') do not match their split parts. It is NOT a match
either when the claim names a holder the reference does not ('the Harbour Times reports X'
against 'X'; a generic holder such as 'critics' does match), when it names all the members of a
set the reference does not close ('the founders were Ada and Ben' against 'the founders
included Ada and Ben'), when it uses a second name only a fact gives (a birth or stage name), or
when its subject points to nothing ('it opened in 1931').

It IS a match when the same value is written another way ('3.4 kg' and '7.5 lb', 'a dozen' and
'12', '25%' and 'a quarter'), and when a change states the result ('raised from $2 to $3' and
'is $3').

Answer 'Entailment' if any reference triplet matches the claim.
Answer 'Contradiction' if the reference states the opposite.
Answer 'Neutral' otherwise.

Give a short explanation and a verdict for every claim id. Never skip a claim.
